newsitem.title: KENYA: Amnesty urges firm U.N. stand on Zaire probe.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty urges firm U.N. stand on Zaire probe.

text.p: Human rights group Amnesty International urged the United Nations on Thursday to stand firm on its probe into reported killings of Rwandan Hutu refugees in the former Zaire.
U.S.-based Physicians for Human Rights (PHR) meanwhile said killings of Rwandan refugees in the former Zaire and western Rwanda continued with Rwandan soldiers often identified as the killers.

Amnesty said U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan should resist pressure from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the former Zaire, to replace a team sent to investigate reported massacres of Rwandan refugees between October last year and May.
Western governments, while in public decrying reported massacres, were privately putting pressure on Annan to compromise the investigation's original mandate, Amnesty said.
"The U.N. should not allow the DRC government to dictate the composition, terms of reference and mandate of any mission to investigate serious human rights violations in the country," Amnesty said.
Annan is expected soon to name a new team to fly to Kinshasa to investigate the massacre reports after DRC President Laurent Kabila blocked the initial team led by Roberto Garreton of Chile.

Rwanda's Vice-President and Defence Minister Major-General Paul Kagame defended on Wednesday Kabila's demands that Garreton be replaced and the team's mission be widened to include killings back until 1993.
The government refused to accept responsibility for abuses committed before it came to power on May 17, Amnesty said.
"We question whether the government of the DRC is genuinely committed to such investigations," the group said.
Kagame has told the Washington Post that Rwandan troops took part in Kabila's rebellion in the former Zaire but has denied they took part in the reported massacres of Rwandan refugees there.

"The killing of Rwandan refugees in Congo and of Congolese villagers continues, with Rwandan soldiers often identified as the perpetrators," the Boston-based Physicians for Human Rights said in a statement.

It said a PHR report based on a two-week mission to the DRC and western Rwanda in June 1997 was presented on Wednesday to a hearing convened by the House of Representatives International Relations Committee.
PHR said it called on U.S. officials to acknowledge the presence of Rwandan troops in the DRC and to insist that those engaged in abuses should be removed and disciplined by Kigali.
It also said Rwandan troops had killed up to 3,000 civilians in western Rwanda in a campaign against Hutu rebels in the last three years. It said PHR investigators were harassed by Rwandan soldiers.
The rebellion in the west has grown since 600,000 Hutu refugees returned home from east Zaire camps last November at the start of Kabila's campaign to oust President Mobutu Sese Seko.

"The under-reported civil war in western Rwanda has had devastating consequences for civilians, with 2,000 to 3,000 killed by the Rwanda army's counterinsurgency campaign in the last three months alone," PHR said.
Aid workers say they are convinced that during the campaign Kabila's troops and their Rwandan allies participated in killings of thousands and possibly tens of thousands of Hutu refugees.
